subject: sociology
chapter_title: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society

concepts.title: Social Change: Types, Causes and the Role of Resistance
concepts.definition: Social change is the transformation over time of institutions, relationships and patterns of living. It arrives through many doors -- technology, economy, environment, ideas and social movements -- and it always meets friction, for established interests and habits resist rearrangement. Change is uneven: some domains race ahead while others lag.
concepts.key_idea: Nothing social stands still -- but change travels unevenly and always drags resistance behind it.

solution_steps.explain: Locate the source -- a new technology, economic shift, ecological pressure, new ideas or organised movement.

Identify who gains and who loses, for resistance is proportional to threatened interests and habits.

concepts.title: Social Order: The Made Regularity of Social Life
concepts.definition: Social order is the patterned predictability of social life -- the fact that traffic flows, queues hold and offices run. Sociologists stress it is an accomplishment, not a natural state: it is produced and maintained by authority, accepted rules and often by coercion, and it can break down in revolution, war or crisis.
concepts.key_idea: Order is not the absence of change but its management -- made, kept, and breakable.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy202.txt lines 140-260 (social order, evolution and spontaneity arguments, authority and coercion, why orders break down, nature and society order)
question_patterns: what is meant by social order and how is it maintained

solution_steps.explain: Order appears as the dependable repetition of roles and routines in a society.
Ask what keeps it -- legitimacy and voluntary compliance, backed where needed by coercion and surveillance.
When legitimacy drains away or force falters, orders crack -- revolutions and breakdowns reveal order's made character.

concepts.title: Village, Town and City: Rural and Urban Life Compared
concepts.definition: Rural society is marked by small scale, proximity and dense face-to-face ties -- everyone knows everyone, and agriculture anchors life. Urban society is larger, denser and more heterogeneous, specialised and anonymous, with formal rules filling the gaps that intimacy fills in villages. Each also changes the other through migration, media and markets.
concepts.key_idea: Village life runs on familiarity, city life on anonymity and rules -- two social worlds in continuous exchange.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy202.txt lines 260-400 (rural and urban society, village characteristics, city characteristics, rural urban differences, migration and linkages)
question_patterns: distinguish rural and urban societies in terms of social relationships

solution_steps.explain: Villages are small and intimate; cities are large, heterogeneous and segmental in relationships.
Village order rests on community opinion and custom; urban order leans on formal law, police and impersonal rules.
Migrants carry cities to villages and villages to cities; remittances, media and markets knit the two worlds together.

worked_examples.q: Which society runs on dense face-to-face ties: rural or urban?

concepts.title: Ecology of the City and Rural Change
concepts.definition: Cities are built environments where geography, economy and planning interact: land use sorts into commercial, industrial and residential zones, shaped by transport and profit. Villages too are changing -- new crops, roads, schooling and communications dissolve the timeless-village image, making both rural and urban worlds works in progress.
concepts.key_idea: The city is a planned-and-sprawl ecology; the village is no museum -- both are mid-change landscapes.
concepts.textbook_ref: kesy202.txt lines 400-520 (ecology of the city, land use, zones, rural change, new agriculture, impact of communications and transport)
question_patterns: what is the ecology of a city and what shapes land use

solution_steps.explain: Commerce clusters at accessible centres, industry near transport links, residences around and between -- ecology shaped by access and price.
Roads, schools, tractors and phones have reworked village economy and hierarchy -- the village changes with the nation.
Urban growth draws rural labour and produce; rural prosperity feeds urban markets -- one changing system, two settings.

worked_examples.q: Sorting land into commercial, industrial and residential use is called what?

worked_examples.question_pattern: A state introduces land ownership ceilings to redistribute land. Identify the sources of change involved and explain why resistance follows.

solution_template.explain: The reform is a state-led change in the economic and legal base of rural life.
Redistribution alters who farms, who commands labour and who wields local authority -- structure follows the land.
Large owners losing land, and custom anchored to it, resist through courts, evasion and politics -- change and counter-pressures in one field.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A theft in a village is settled by the elders; the same theft in a metro is reported to the police. Explain the difference in social order using the rural-urban contrast.

solution_template.explain: Small, dense acquaintance lets elders act as moral authority -- order through community opinion and custom.
Anonymity rules out elder moral reach, so order shifts to formal law and police procedure.
The same disorder meets different order-machines: personalised control in the village, impersonal control in the city.
